title: Assist in farm planning and layout for conservation and rainwater harvesting

lessons.title: Planning a farm layout for conservation
lessons.html:
Why plan for conservation?

Rain in much of South Africa falls in short, heavy storms. On bare or poorly laid-out land, water runs off quickly, carrying topsoil and leaving dongas, while the soil stays dry. Conservation planning arranges land use so that water is slowed, spread and soaked into the soil, and erosion is prevented.

Reading the land

  • Slope: steep slopes erode easily and are best kept under permanent cover such as veld, pasture or trees.
  • Soil types: deep, well-drained soils for crops; shallow or wet soils for grazing or conservation.
  • Water flow: watch where runoff goes in a storm, where it collects and where gullies start.
  • Wetlands and rivers: must be protected with buffer strips.
  • Existing infrastructure: roads, fences, buildings, dams.

Land capability

Land is classed by what it can safely support. A layout plan places each use on suitable land: arable crops on gentle, deep soils; grazing on steeper or shallower land; non-arable areas such as rocky ridges and wetlands left for conservation. Under the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983, cultivating unsuitable land such as wetlands or very steep slopes is restricted.

Conservation structures

  • Contour banks (terraces): earth banks across the slope that intercept runoff and lead it slowly to a waterway.
  • Grassed waterways: broad, grassed channels that carry excess water safely downslope.
  • Diversion banks: divert runoff away from lands, roads or buildings.
  • Contour planting and strip cropping: rows and strips follow the contour.
  • Gully control: stone packs, brush packs or small check dams to slow water and trap soil in existing gullies.

Roads and fences should follow contours or ridges where possible; tracks running straight downhill become erosion channels.

lessons.title: Rainwater harvesting and marking out contours
lessons.html:
Rainwater harvesting methods

  • Roof harvesting: gutters lead rain from sheds and houses into tanks. Clean gutters, use a first-flush diverter, cover tanks and fit overflow pipes.
  • In-field rainwater harvesting: small basins or runoff strips between crop rows catch rain and direct it to the root zone. Used in dryland vegetable and maize production.
  • Swales and contour ridges: shallow trenches on contour that hold water so it soaks in.
  • Small earth dams and ponds: store runoff for livestock or irrigation. Dams on watercourses may need authorisation under the National Water Act 36 of 1998, so check with the manager before building.
  • Mulching and cover: keeps rain in the soil and reduces evaporation.

Marking out contours

A contour is a line of equal height along a slope. Simple tools:

  • A-frame: a wooden frame with a plumb line or spirit level. When both legs touch level ground the line hangs at the centre mark. Walk it across the slope, marking points with pegs.
  • Water tube level: a clear hose filled with water; the water level is equal at both ends.
  • Dumpy level or GPS: used by surveyors and advisers for larger works.

Steps to assist

  1. Clear the line of obstacles.
  2. Start at a marked point and walk across the slope with the A-frame, pegging every few metres.
  3. Smooth sharp bends in the line of pegs.
  4. Space lines down the slope as instructed; steeper slopes need closer spacing.
  5. Dig or plough along the pegged line as directed.

Maintenance

After storms, check banks for breaks and overtopping, waterways for scouring, and tanks for leaks. Repair small damage early.

Safety

Be careful on steep slopes and near dam walls. Use tools properly, wear boots and gloves, and keep clear of machinery building banks.

Key points

  • Plan land use according to slope, soil and water flow.
  • Use contour banks, grassed waterways and diversion banks to control runoff.
  • Harvest rain from roofs, in fields and in swales or dams.
  • Mark contours with an A-frame or water tube level.
  • Inspect and repair structures after storms.
